records.sourceFile: The NFL orthopaedic surgery     outcomes database - The    effect of common orthopaedic procedures on     football   careers.pdf

paper.citation: Mai HT, Alvarez AP, Freshman RD, Chun DS, Minhas SV, Patel AA, et al. The NFL Orthopaedic Surgery Outcomes Database (NO-SOD): The Effect of Common Orthopaedic Procedures on Football Careers. Am J Sports Med. 2016 (published online June 16, 2016).
paper.abstract: A case series of NFL athletes who had one of ten common orthopaedic procedures between 2003 and 2013, identified from team injury reports, press releases and other public records. Return to play, games played, career length and a standardised performance score were compared before and after surgery.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players (79%) returned to play after common orthopaedic surgery, but patellar tendon repair had the lowest return rate (50%). ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and lasting drops in performance.
paper.methods: Retrospective case series of 559 NFL athletes who were on an active roster or injured reserve at the time of surgery, confirmed by two sources. Return to play was defined as at least one regular-season game after surgery, and a position-specific performance score was compared with the season before injury. Offensive linemen and special teams players were excluded from the performance analysis, and procedures with fewer than 25 cases were excluded.
paper.findings: Overall return to play was 79.4% (range 50.0% to 96.3%). Return was highest after forearm ORIF (96.3%), tibia IMN (90.9%) and sports hernia repair (90.2%), and lowest after patellar tendon repair (50.0%). Post-surgery career length was 1.6 years after ACL reconstruction and 1.5 years after patellar tendon repair. Performance fell in the first season after ACL reconstruction, Achilles repair, patellar tendon repair and tibia IMN, and stayed down after ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair; players who stayed in the league for seasons 2 and 3 returned to baseline games played.
paper.limitations: Public-source data may miss some injuries, and players who left the league for non-medical reasons may be counted as not returning. Retirement confounds the post-surgery figures, the performance score excludes offensive linemen and special teams players, and the study does not compare rehabilitation protocols.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use procedure-specific return rates and career outcomes to set realistic expectations and counsel players, especially after patellar tendon repair or ACL reconstruction. A first-season dip in games and performance is expected after several procedures, and performance did not recover after ACL reconstruction or patellar tendon repair.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the first-season performance drop after ACL reconstruction, Achilles repair, patellar tendon repair and tibia IMN to plan a graded return and monitor output after surgery. The study has no data on specific training or load, so it does not set training prescriptions.
paper.rtp: This study is directly about return to play in professional players: 79% returned overall, 50% after patellar tendon repair, and ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and sustained performance losses. It does not compare rehabilitation protocols, so it cannot show which rehabilitation approach improves return.

records.sourceFile: The Use of Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating Recovery After Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes - A Scoping Review.pdf

paper.citation: DiCesare R, Tahir U, Noori A, Matthies NF, Chahal J, Paul RA, et al. The Use of Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating Recovery After Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes: A Scoping Review. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(11):23259671251387342.
paper.abstract: A scoping review of 12 studies (319 athletes, 34% female) on how DEXA has been used to track bone mineral density and body composition during recovery from musculoskeletal injury. Bone density fell after injury, mostly in the injured limb, and some rehabilitation approaches preserved bone and lean mass better than others.
paper.tldr: DEXA can track bone and lean-mass loss after musculoskeletal injury in athletes. Bone density often fell 4-10% in the first 6 months and showed partial to near-complete recovery over 12-25 months after ACL injury, but the evidence is small and mostly observational, so DEXA is a monitoring tool rather than a return-to-play test.
paper.methods: PRISMA-ScR scoping review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL and SportDISCUS (2000-2024) with two reviewers screening independently. Included studies had athletes with musculoskeletal injury, a baseline DEXA scan near the injury site and at least one follow-up scan. Because designs were heterogeneous, the results were synthesised narratively.
paper.findings: Of 1132 unique records, 12 studies were included, seven of them on ACL reconstruction. Bone mineral density typically fell about 4-10% in the first 6 months after injury or surgery and was near baseline by 24 months in several ACL studies, and injured limbs lost about 7-14% lean mass during immobilisation before partial to full recovery. In the one randomised trial (17 athletes with blood flow restriction, 15 controls), time to return to sport was shorter with blood flow restriction (6.42 vs 8.30 months), and that group kept lean mass and lost less bone.
paper.limitations: Most studies were observational or single-case reports with small samples, and the authors did not run a formal risk-of-bias assessment. The abstract says that running plus isometric exercise better preserved bone density than conventional programs, but the body reports no conventional comparison for that protocol, so that claim is not supported in the text. The authors also note that DEXA can overestimate trunk lean mass compared with MRI.
paper.practicalImplications: Serial DEXA scans can show whether an injured limb is losing or regaining bone and lean mass, which can guide loading and rehabilitation intensity. Blood flow restriction is worth discussing when faster return and better lean-mass retention matter, but that rests on one small trial.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Baseline and serial DEXA scans can track limb asymmetry in lean mass during rehabilitation. A cited soccer study found no significant correlation between body composition asymmetry and injury, only marginal associations, and the review measures no performance outcomes, so it does not show that DEXA-guided programming improves performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: DEXA-measured bone and lean-mass recovery can be read alongside strength and functional tests when planning return to sport after ACL reconstruction or stress injury. The review cannot set return-to-play thresholds, because the authors state that validated thresholds are still needed and most evidence is observational.

records.sourceFile: The Use of Fantasy Points to Evaluate Return-to-Play Performance After Time-Loss Injuries in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Angileri HS, Geier JA, Hadley SM Jr, McLoughlin DE, Owen MM, May JM, et al. The Use of Fantasy Points to Evaluate Return-to-Play Performance After Time-Loss Injuries in the National Football League. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e99333.
paper.abstract: Retrospective descriptive epidemiology study of time-loss injuries in NFL offensive skill players over five seasons (2017 to 2022), comparing fantasy points per game in the injury year with the following season. Reported injuries were associated with a decline of -0.50 PPG (CI -0.67 to -0.33), with the largest declines for quarterbacks and for players with more than three years in the league.
paper.tldr: Fantasy points per game fell by about 0.5 on average in the season after a time-loss injury, with the largest drop for quarterbacks. Fantasy points may be a low-cost, publicly available trend to watch, but they do not replace clinical return-to-play assessment.
paper.methods: Retrospective descriptive study of injuries to quarterbacks, running backs, wide receivers, tight ends and fullbacks that caused at least one missed game over five NFL seasons, using public injury and statistics sources. Return to performance was the change in fantasy PPG between the injury year and the following season, with injured players' totals normalized to games played.
paper.findings: The overall change was -0.50 PPG (CI -0.67 to -0.33). Quarterbacks declined by -1.95 PPG (CI -3.47 to -0.44) and wide receivers by -0.33 PPG; running backs declined by -0.7 PPG and fullbacks by -0.09 PPG. Shin (-3.24 PPG) and arm (-2.65 PPG) injuries had the largest declines, but their CIs cross zero. Games missed were not associated with PPG change (R2 = 0.0047). Injuries after a bye week were associated with a -1.22 PPG change, while injuries before a bye week were associated with a +0.25 PPG change.
paper.limitations: Public, retrospective data with no severity detail (for example, sprain versus fracture), and games missed was not a usable severity proxy. Coaching, scheme, opposition and weather changes were not adjusted for. Injuries were counted separately when a player had more than one, and some values are inconsistent: the abstract says bye-week timing did not alter PPG, but Table 3 reports a CI (0.018 to 0.474) that excludes zero, and some CI bounds in Table 3 contain typographical errors. The tenure effect (-17.10 PPG, CI -21.61 to -12.59) is implausibly large and should be read with caution.
paper.practicalImplications: Fantasy point trends may be added as a low-cost, objective supplement when following an offensive skill player's output after a time-loss injury, alongside clinical assessment. Position and injury location are useful context for expectations, with the caveat that the shin and arm estimates are imprecise.
paper.athleteDev: Fantasy points per game may give a rough, publicly available performance trend to compare with a player's pre-injury level. The study reports group averages, not individual readiness, so it cannot set training loads or prescribe a progression.
paper.rtp: The study can inform expectations that offensive skill players, especially quarterbacks, often produce fewer fantasy points in the season after a time-loss injury. It cannot show when an athlete is ready to return or whether recovery is complete, because fantasy points do not reflect injury severity and clinical evaluation is still needed.

records.sourceFile: The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthend hamstring position after hamstring strain injury.pdf

paper.citation: Nara G, Samukawa M, Oba K, Koshino Y, Ishida T, Kasahara S, et al. The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthened hamstring position after hamstring strain injury. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022;53:91-96.
paper.abstract: Compared isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, and hamstring flexibility, between the limbs of 14 male athletes with a history of hamstring strain injury and 14 controls. Peak torque was lower in the previously injured limb at 30 degrees only, and rate of torque development and flexibility did not differ between limbs.
paper.tldr: Athletes with a past hamstring strain still had lower isometric knee flexor strength in the injured leg, but only when the hamstring was stretched at 30 degrees of knee flexion. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study. Participants with a history of HSI (self-reported, all returned to full training) and controls had isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development measured on an isokinetic dynamometer at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, seated with the hip at 85 degrees. Hamstring flexibility was measured with the active knee extension test. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests.
paper.findings: In the HSI group, peak torque in the injured limb was lower than in the uninjured limb at 30 degrees (P = 0.037, d = 0.55), with no difference at 60 or 90 degrees. Peak rate of torque development showed no limb differences at any angle, and active knee extension did not differ between limbs. The control group showed no between-limb differences in peak torque.
paper.limitations: Injury was self-reported and mostly not diagnosed by a physician, so injury location and severity are unknown, and 64% of participants had no rehabilitation. Only male athletes were studied, time since injury varied from 1 month to 7 years, and four participants' injured side was non-dominant. The design is cross-sectional, and hip extensor activity and muscle architecture were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Isometric knee flexor testing with the hip flexed and the knee at 30 degrees may show strength deficits that a standard hip-neutral or 0-degree test could miss. Isometric training at a lengthened hamstring range can be started early in rehabilitation, with pain monitored, as the authors suggest. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs, so it did not add information in this sample.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Strength staff can use a 30-degree isometric knee flexor test with the hip flexed to check between-leg strength in athletes with prior hamstring strain, and include lengthened-position isometric work in their hamstring programme. The study measured strength only, with no sprint or match performance outcomes, so it does not show that these changes improve on-field performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study shows that some athletes who have returned to full training still have lower isometric knee flexor strength at a lengthened hamstring position, so testing at that angle could be added to return-to-sport review. It cannot set a return-to-sport cut-off, because the design is cross-sectional and does not show that the deficit predicts reinjury.
